strengths: First systematic theoretical treatment of false-positive cluster/outlier artifacts in t-SNE, filling an explicitly identified gap in prior work (which focused on true-positive guarantees for well-separated inputs).

Clean and rigorous mathematical development: the identification of t-SNE's invariance to both multiplicative and additive rescaling of squared interpoint distances (via a clever application of the Schoenberg embedding theorem) is a novel and illuminating structural insight that unifies the main results.

Results are stated generally and shown to hold across multiple standard cluster-validity indices (silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn), strengthening the claim that the phenomenon is not an artifact of a particular metric.

Strong complementary empirical validation on both synthetic and real-world datasets (single-cell PBMC genomics, credit-card fraud, BBC news RoBERTa embeddings), showing the theoretical failure modes (impostor datasets, poison-point attacks, outlier masking) are practically realizable, not just adversarial curiosities.
The outlier suppression result (Theorem 8) gives a clean, input-agnostic bound and is supported by a compelling contrast with PCA on real fraud-detection data.
Practical relevance is well-articulated: implications for downstream scientific interpretation (e.g., genomics, anomaly/fraud detection) are clearly discussed.
Code availability supports reproducibility, and proofs are relegated to a thorough appendix, keeping the main text readable.
weaknesses: The main constructive theorems (3, 5, 6) rely on the very permissive notion of 'stationary point' (any critical point of the KL objective), not the actual output of gradient descent with early exaggeration as run in practice; it is not fully established that the constructed adversarial/impostor datasets are reachable by standard t-SNE optimization procedures (initialization + early exaggeration + gradient descent), which somewhat weakens the practical bite of the pure existence results, even though the empirical sections partially address this gap.

The dimensionality assumption D = n-1 used throughout the theory (needed for the Schoenberg-embedding argument) is quite restrictive relative to typical real-world datasets where D is fixed and much smaller than n; the paper's 'without loss of generality' framing could be misleading and deserves more discussion of how the results degrade or transfer to lower-dimensional, structured inputs.

The theoretical outlier bound (α ≤ 3, Theorem 8) is far looser than what is empirically observed (α rarely exceeds 0.2 in practice); the gap between the theoretical worst case and empirical typical case is not discussed, leaving the practical tightness of the bound unclear.

The paper does not examine whether the identified pathologies (additive invariance, affinity asymmetry) are unique to t-SNE or are shared by related methods (e.g., UMAP), which would help contextualize the significance and generality of the findings.

Limited actionable guidance for practitioners: the discussion section raises the important open question but offers little concrete advice on how to detect or mitigate these failure modes in routine data-analysis workflows.

Some of the density/notational complexity (e.g., the interplay of σ*, perplexity, Definition 1) may hinder accessibility to the broader ML/data-visualization audience who use t-SNE without deep familiarity with its optimization theory.
